prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

For Alexander Moysaenko The black heart of the moon’s visible through the trees from here. Where are you? I’m alone on the road with a dead phone. The birds are flapping overhead but there’s not much light to be guided by. If any horizon becomes visible enough to follow. Forget the rain’s smear, the chafe of fabric at the calf. The money ran out. The diners are stuffed and back for more. Each terrible thing I said to the child will get repeated hopefully as a joke. And like language, these gestures, or a certain way of nodding one’s head, it all eases in with less than a breath. Forget the song’s words, the order of the band’s set tonight. The black moon’s heart’s got that sinister bent and I want to get touched at by the snakes. One of the students in my class used to go bear hunting with his two uncles. They played recordings of distressed animals to lure in tentative animals to kill. This practice is illegal in many places. Because it’s so very effective. I split open the apple and hand the good half to a child on the bus nestled in under the arm of her sleeping mother. Love from here is a long way to go. Get on your bike and ride through the lights.

For Alexander Moysaenko

The moon's black heart is visible through the trees from here. Where are you? I'm alone on the road, my phone dead. Birds flap overhead, though there's scarcely light enough to guide by—if any horizon should become visible enough to follow. Forget the rain's smear, the chafing of fabric against the calf. The money's gone. The diners sit stuffed, then return for more. Every terrible thing I said to the child will, I hope, be repeated someday as a joke. And like language itself—these gestures, this particular way of nodding one's head—it all settles in with less than a breath. Forget the song's lyrics, forget tonight's set order. The black moon's heart carries something sinister, and I want to be touched by the snakes. One of my students used to hunt bear with his two uncles. They'd play recordings of distressed animals to lure in the wary ones, then kill them. The practice is illegal in many places—precisely because it works so well. I split the apple open and hand the better half to a child on the bus, nestled beneath her sleeping mother's arm. Love, from here, is a long way to go. Get on your bike and ride through the lights.
outputs.L2:
For Alexander Moysaenko

Through the branches, I can make out the moon's dark center. Where have you gone? I'm stranded on this road, my phone dead. Overhead, birds beat their wings, though scarcely enough light exists to steer by. Should some horizon emerge clearly enough to trace. Never mind the streak of rain, the rub of cloth against my leg. My funds ran dry. The people at the restaurant, already full, return for seconds. Every awful thing I've told the child will someday, hopefully, become a running joke. Just like speech itself—these small movements, that particular tilt of a head—it all settles into place effortlessly, quicker than a single exhale. Never mind the lyrics to the song, or which act plays when tonight. That dark lunar core carries something ominous, and I crave the sensation of serpents against my skin. A boy in my class once hunted bears alongside his two uncles. They'd broadcast the cries of wounded creatures to draw in wary prey. Such methods are outlawed in numerous regions—precisely because they work so well. I break the apple in two and pass the better piece to a girl on the bus, curled beneath her sleeping mother's arm. From this point, love stretches out far ahead. Mount your bicycle and pedal onward through the streetlamps.
outputs.L3:
# Standing at the Edge of Dark

The speaker finds themselves stranded on a road stretched into darkness, phone dead in hand, with no horizon visible to orient them—no glow of a distant town, no line where land meets sky to promise arrival somewhere. This is a portrait of profound isolation, not merely physical but existential: the tools we rely on for connection have failed, and even nature's most basic assurance—a horizon—has been swallowed by night. The speaker stands not lost in the dramatic sense, but disconnected in a quieter, more unsettling way, untethered from the usual anchors of location and communication alike.

Yet in this moment of vulnerability, the small physical irritations that might normally demand attention—rain soaking through clothing, fabric rubbing raw against skin—are consciously pushed aside. These bodily discomforts, so immediate and insistent in ordinary life, become almost irrelevant here. The speaker chooses instead to let the mind wander toward larger, more consequential matters, as if the darkness itself demands a reckoning with what truly matters rather than what merely irritates.

Among these larger reflections surfaces guilt—specific and gnawing—over harsh words once spoken to a child. The speaker turns this memory over, examining the sting of it, and allows themselves a fragile hope: that time might work its alchemy on this pain, transforming it eventually into something softer, perhaps even into shared laughter or a story told with affection rather than shame. This is the peculiar mercy of memory, that our cruelties and mistakes, however sharp in the moment, might one day be remembered with tenderness rather than regret—though this transformation is never guaranteed, only hoped for.

The poem then pivots to a startling and dark parable: bear hunters who use recordings of animals in distress—their cries of pain or fear—as illegal lures, precisely because such sounds prove devastatingly effective at drawing prey close. This image serves as a stark metaphor for manipulation, for how vulnerability itself can be weaponized, how the very sounds of suffering can be twisted into traps. It suggests something troubling about connection and trust: that what draws us toward one another—empathy, the instinct to respond to another's pain—can be exploited, turned into mechanism rather than genuine encounter. The metaphor casts a shadow over the speaker's own isolation, hinting that even reaching out, even responding to distress, carries the risk of manipulation, of being lured toward harm disguised as need.

And yet the poem does not end in this darkness. It closes instead with small, deliberate gestures of tenderness—the simple act of sharing an apple with a child, a moment of quiet nourishment and connection that stands in direct contrast to the earlier isolation and the disturbing metaphor of the hunters' lures. This small domestic tenderness becomes a kind of answer, however modest, to the vast disconnection described earlier. Alongside this gesture comes a call to keep moving forward, even as love itself feels distant, elusive, perhaps even compromised by the possibility of manipulation suggested in the hunting metaphor. The poem ultimately holds these tensions together: isolation and connection, guilt and hoped-for forgiveness, the danger of vulnerability and the necessity of tenderness anyway. It suggests that even without clear horizons to guide us, without certainty that love is trustworthy or present, we are called to continue—to share the apple, to soften the guilt, to keep walking the dark road forward.
outputs.L4:
**Through the Lights**

The road is dark and I am walking it alone,
phone dead in my pocket like a stone
I carry out of habit. No one to call
even if it woke. The moon comes through the trees
in pieces, the way memory comes—
not whole, never whole, just enough light
to make out shapes.

Something moves overhead. Birds,
maybe, returning to wherever birds return to
when the sky starts closing.
I don't look up in time to see them,
only hear the disturbance they leave in the leaves,
a rustling like something being taken back.

I think of the boy I was harsh with once—
not mine, but close enough to feel like mine,
the way children who aren't yours
still carry the weight of what you say.
I don't remember the words now,
only his face doing that thing faces do
when they're deciding whether to believe you.
I would take it back if taking back
were a road instead of a memory,
if I could walk backward through the dark
the way I'm walking forward through it now.

A student told me once about the men
who hunt bears with the sound of a cub crying—
recorded, played back into the woods,
the mother coming because a mother comes,
because that sound is the one sound
she cannot leave unanswered.
It's illegal, he said, like that mattered,
like the law was the wound instead of the trap.
I think about this more than I should.
I think about all the calls we answer
that are not what they seem,
and all the ones that are.

On the bus once, a girl fell asleep
against the window, her daughter awake beside her,
maybe four years old, holding a small toy
too tightly, the way children hold things
they're afraid of losing.
I didn't know them. I would never know them.
But I reached over, just slightly,
and steadied the mother's arm
so it wouldn't slip from around the child
when the bus turned.
That was all. That was everything I had to give
in that moment, and I gave it
without being seen giving it,
which is maybe the only kind of giving
that counts.

I don't know how these things fit together—
the dead phone, the moon in pieces,
the birds I didn't see, the boy's face,
the bear coming to a sound that wasn't her cub,
the sleeping mother's arm.
Maybe they don't fit. Maybe the fitting
is not the point. Maybe the point
is only this: that even in the dark,
even with no way to call for help
or forgiveness, even knowing
that love is sometimes a recording
played to lure something out of hiding,
love is still what we're hunting for,
still what hunts us,
still the thing worth walking toward
even when the road is nothing
but the absence of light.

So I keep walking. The trees break open
ahead of me—not stars, just streetlights,
ordinary and human, holding their small ground
against the dark.
I go toward them
the way the bear must have gone,
the way the child held her toy,
the way I should have gone toward the boy
instead of away.

Through the lights, then.
Not because I know what's on the other side,
but because this is what the living do—
we walk through the lights
we're given,
however far apart they stand,
however dim,
carrying what tenderness we have
like something recorded,
like something that might still call
another heart out of the trees.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem dedicated to someone named Alexander Moysaenko, incorporating imagery of the moon, birds, and a dead phone.
counterfactuals.output:
# For Alexander Moysaenko, Who Does Not Answer

Somewhere the moon is dialing your number
with its one cold finger of light,
patient as a switchboard operator
who has worked the night shift since the Flood.

Alexander, the birds have your voicemail memorized.
They recite it at 4 a.m.
in a language made of static and wingbeat,
perched on the black obelisk
of your phone, which lies face-down
in the grass like a stone
that used to be a mirror.

The moon keeps calling.
It has nothing to say—
only wants to hear the ringing
go on forever, unanswered,
a bell underwater,
a heart that learned to toll
without a body around it.

Somewhere you are folding paper birds
out of the missed-call notifications,
Alexander, and letting them go
into a sky the color of a dead screen,
that particular black
that isn't night, isn't nothing,
just *off*—

and still the moon leans closer,
an ear pressed to the door
of a house where the phone
rings and rings
in a room no one has entered
since the last bird
flew out of the receiver
and became a satellite,
became a rumor,
became the sound
your name makes
when no one
is left
to say it.

The battery is at zero.
The moon does not care.
It has all the time
that was ever taken
from you, Alexander—
it is spending it now,
coin by coin,
into a phone
that will never
light up again,
into a silence
shaped exactly
like your listening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary poem with fragmented, dreamlike imagery that shifts between personal memory, nature, and small acts of kindness toward strangers.
counterfactuals.output:
**Weather Systems**

My mother's hands in dishwater, 1994—
                    no, that's not right,
the water was somewhere else,
                                        a lake maybe,
green-black and cold enough to stop a heart
if you stayed too long.

*

A woman on the 6 train offers her seat
to no one in particular. Just stands,
holds the pole like a maypole,
like she's dancing alone
in a field only she remembers.

*

Snow falls on the parking lot
where I learned to drive,
my father's voice a low radio
tuned to a station that no longer exists.
                              *Ease off the brake, slowly, slowly—*

The world keeps doing this:
handing me back pieces
of a year I thought I'd spent.

*

Somewhere a heron stands
in water up to its knees,
patient as a held breath,
and somewhere else
a boy gives his umbrella
to a stranger at a bus stop,
walks home soaked,
grinning like he's gotten away
with something holy.

*

I keep almost remembering
the smell of my grandmother's kitchen—
cardamom, or maybe just sugar burning,
the window fogged with the day's first coffee,
her hand on my head,
                              light as a moth landing.

*

The mail carrier stops
to help an old man pick up
the oranges that rolled from his bag,
the sun doing that thing
where it turns everything
briefly, unbearably gold.

*

I don't know where the dream ends
and the actual snow begins.
I don't know if my father said
*ease off the brake*
or if I invented him saying it,
building a father
out of static and longing.

*

Someone somewhere is being kind
to someone they'll never see again.
This has always been true.
It is true right now,
in a language I don't speak,
in a country I've never seen,
someone's coat around someone's shoulders,

*

and the lake is still there, greenly,
holding the shape of my mother's hands,
and the heron hasn't moved,
and I am still learning
how to ease off the brake
of my own life,
slowly,
                    slowly,
into whatever this is—
                              morning, maybe.
Or memory dressed as morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a literary journal submission, addressed "For [a name]," blending night imagery, a lost child's laughter, and a story about illegal hunting practices.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Dark Keeps**

*For Inès*

Night comes down like a net thrown over the orchard,
and somewhere in its mesh a child's laugh
still snags—bright, unaccountable,
the sound of someone who is no longer
anywhere I can call.

I keep this poem the way my father
kept his rifle: oiled, illegal,
wrapped in a feed sack behind the woodstove,
because some hungers outlast the seasons
that are meant to hold them.

He'd go out past the fence line after midnight,
flashlight taped to give a narrower beam,
and the deer would freeze the way memory does—
caught mid-motion, eyes like wet stones,
believing stillness was a kind of safety.

I was young enough to think this was devotion:
the quiet trucks, the unlicensed dogs,
the way men spoke of quotas
like weather they'd outsmarted.
I did not yet know how much of love
is only appetite with better manners.

Somewhere in that same dark
a girl was laughing on a swing set
two farms over, chain-creak and delight,
and the sound carried the way gunfire does—
farther than it should, changing shape
as it goes, becoming something
almost like music, almost like grief.

I don't know why these things nest together
in whatever chamber holds a life:
the doe's small collapse into brush,
my father's hands, quick and practiced,
that laughter I can no longer place
a face to, only a season,
only the specific navy of that sky.

Inès, this is what the night keeps—
not innocence, which was never
really the question,
but the exact weight of what we take
without asking, and call it need,
and how the taken world
goes on laughing somewhere just out of reach,
as if nothing here were final,
as if the fence line held.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem that mixes an unreliable narrator's night journey with a strange anecdote about a student and bear hunting, ending on a tender, hopeful note.
counterfactuals.output:
# Notes Found in a Coat Pocket, Undated

I.

I left the house at the hour when clocks
apologize for themselves,
walking or not-walking, I can't be sure—
memory is a dog that brings back
the wrong stick every time.

The streetlamps kept lying about the distance.
I told them I forgave them anyway.

*

There was a student once—I may have invented her,
or she invented me, we're still deciding—
who signed up for a course called
*Practical Ethics of the Wilderness*
and ended up, through some clerical error
in the registrar's cold heart,
on a bear hunt in Vermont with three men
named after Old Testament weather.

She had never held a rifle.
She held it like a question
she wasn't ready to answer.

II.

The night kept folding into itself
like a letter no one will send.
I passed a house that might have been my childhood
or someone else's, borrowed,
the way dreams borrow furniture
from stores that closed years ago.

*

The bear, when it came, was smaller than the legend—
aren't they always—
and the student lowered the gun
and said, *I just wanted to see*
and the men, who had killed before,
who wore killing like a good coat,
went quiet in a way that wasn't shame,
exactly, but close,
the way a hymn is close to a scream
if you slow it down enough.

III.

I don't know if I'm the one walking
or the one being walked,
some nights the sidewalk
is the only honest thing in the story.

*

The bear ambled off into whatever bears go into—
theology, maybe, or just more forest—
and the student stood there
holding an unfired question
and started, quietly, to laugh,
not at the bear, not at the men,
but at the sheer fact
of being alive and unprepared
for the size of the world's mercy.

IV.

I think I am close to home now.
I think home is a rumor
I've decided to trust.

*

Here is what I want to tell you,
whoever finds this coat,
whoever unfolds this paper
like a small wet flag of surrender:

somewhere a girl put down a gun
because looking was enough,
because the world, for one long breath,
did not need to be conquered,
only witnessed—

and somewhere, I hope, a door
is left unlocked for me,
a light still on,
someone who knows
which of my stories are true
and loves me
in spite of, and because of,
all the ones that aren't.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a moody, introspective poem for a dedication page that juxtaposes solitude and darkness with small human tenderness, using repeated imagery of a "black moon" and instructions like "forget."
counterfactuals.output:
*for the ones who stayed in the dark with me*

---

Forget the porch light, the easy moths,
the way morning arrives without asking.

Forget the sound of your own name
said kindly.

There is a black moon that follows certain people—
not the absence of light
but light turned inward, hoarding itself,
a held breath in the shape of a sky.

I have lived under it so long
I mistook it for a roof.

Forget the calendars, the years
that stack like unread mail.

But remember this:
someone once put a hand
against the small of my back
in a room with no windows,
and did not ask me to be anything
but tired.

The black moon does not apologize.
It only rises, the way grief rises,
the way love sometimes has to—
sideways, unannounced,
mistaken at first for another kind of loss.

Forget the year this was written.
Forget the reasons.

Remember only:
two people,
a dark table,
a small warmth passed between hands
like a coin neither of us could spend
but both of us kept.

This is for you—
under whatever black moon you're carrying,
in whatever room has gone quiet.

Forget that I am far away.
Remember that I am still looking up,
finding the same unlit sky,
and thinking of you
like a lamp
I refuse to let go out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
